title: Never know who will touch you dead. Wash and shampoo. I believe they clip the nails and the hair. Keep a bit in an envelope. Grows all the same after. Unclean job.
html_source:
I think Bloom is musing about Catholicism and Judaism. In Judaism, a deceased body is always guarded, never left alone. Washing the body is a ritual, considered a mitzvah, and done in conjunction with prayers and blessings. To just leave this job to the women of the town or family, to leave the corpse unattended, and to not follow the rituals would be considered “unclean”, or not in accordance with Kosher laws in their broader application. A devout Jew may not know specifically who might touch him dead, but is assured that he will be treated with respect and reverence.

Cutting and disposing of fingernails is also ritualistic in Judaism, though I don’t know what is to be done with the nail and hair clippings of the deceased. I don’t imagine keeping them in an envelope is approved.

Interesting that his musings are about shampoo, washing, and cleanliness – and he is transported from being “in his head” back to the physical world by the reality of the soap in his pocket.
